title: On Losing Someone You Love
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: Writing from the loss of his grandmother, the author of Stoic Wisdoms sets out to correct the caricature of Stoicism as cold and emotionless. That reputation, he argues, comes from misread fragments — Epictetus on kissing your child as though they might die, the mistranslation of apatheia as 'no feelings,' and the morbid-sounding practice of premeditatio malorum — whereas the tradition actually distinguished the involuntary first wave of grief, which no philosophy should try to legislate away, from the judgments we add afterward. Drawing on Seneca's letters and his Consolation to Marcia, the essay names two betrayals of grief: suppression, which retroactively denies the love was real, and clinging, which builds an identity around the wound and preserves the person as an emblem of suffering rather than a continuing influence. Grieving well, he concludes, means holding both truths at once — the grief is permitted because the love was real, and the softening is permitted because the love continues, in a changed form, in how we live and treat others.
points: The 'cold Stoic' reputation rests on three misreadings: Epictetus quoted out of context, apatheia mistranslated as having no feelings, and premeditatio malorum mistaken for morbidity.
Later Stoics distinguished the involuntary first wave of grief (the gasp, the tears) from the judgments added afterward; only what comes after is open to evaluation.
Seneca holds that to feel no grief at a friend's loss would mean we never really had the friend — the grief is evidence the love was real.
The two betrayals of grief are suppression (a daily small denial that the love existed) and clinging (letting grief 'acquire a domicile in the mind' and become identity).
Grieving well means carrying the person forward as a continuing influence — the values and gestures they left in us — rather than keeping the wound intact out of misplaced loyalty.
quotes: Grief does that. It returns the person to you in a different form, after you no longer have them in the form you were used to.
What they offered, and what I want to pass on as carefully as I can, is a way of thinking about grief that doesn’t shame you for feeling it and doesn’t trap you inside it.
The tears are not the problem. Pretending the tears shouldn’t be there is one kind of problem. Building a life around the tears is another kind of problem.

The grief is the evidence that the love was real. Removing the grief would mean removing the love retrospectively, which is exactly the move the caricature accuses Stoicism of recommending and which the actual tradition consistently refused.
Grief that stays a wound asks nothing of you except that you keep it.
The grief is evidence the love was real. The love produced something in you that survives the loss. What survives is what they gave.
That the dead go on shaping the living, in small daily ways, if the living let them.
